body_markdown:
More than 120 NHS workers have secured nearly £750,000 in compensation following prolonged exposure to unsafe nitrous oxide levels at Basildon Hospital.


## Introduction


A serious workplace safety failure at Basildon University Hospital in Essex has resulted in a compensation settlement worth almost £750,000 for 121 NHS employees. The staff, including 85 midwives, reportedly experienced prolonged exposure to excessive levels of nitrous oxide while working in the hospital's maternity unit between 2021 and 2023.


The incident has raised significant concerns about workplace safety, hospital maintenance, communication and the responsibility of NHS organisations to protect their employees. Workers reported symptoms including headaches, fatigue and brain fog after potentially dangerous levels of the gas were detected in their working environment.


The settlement has been described as a landmark outcome by the Royal College of Midwives (RCM), which has called for stronger action to prevent similar incidents across maternity services.


## What Happened at Basildon Hospital?


According to reports, staff at Basildon University Hospital were exposed to elevated concentrations of nitrous oxide because of ventilation problems and leaking gas pipelines in the maternity unit.


Nitrous oxide is commonly used in maternity care as part of gas and air, a pain relief option offered to women during labour. When medical equipment operates correctly and appropriate ventilation is maintained, this mixture is widely used in childbirth.


However, the circumstances at Basildon Hospital were different. Investigations found that the gas had accumulated to levels that exceeded the recommended workplace exposure limit.


Routine monitoring in June 2021 reportedly identified concerning readings. Some measurements exceeded 1,000 parts per million, while one reportedly approached 3,000 parts per million. The recognised long-term workplace exposure limit cited in the report is 100 parts per million.


An internal hospital report indicated that some employees may have been exposed to concentrations as much as 30 times above the applicable workplace limit during the period under investigation.


These findings highlighted the potential seriousness of the situation and the importance of functioning ventilation systems, effective monitoring and prompt action when safety concerns arise.


## More Than 120 NHS Workers Receive Compensation


A total of 121 members of staff pursued legal claims following their exposure to the gas. The group included 85 midwives who had continued providing care to women and newborn babies while working in the affected maternity environment.


The settlement, worth almost £750,000, represents a significant development for the affected employees. However, financial compensation cannot necessarily reverse the consequences of exposure or remove the uncertainty some workers may feel about their health.


Daniel Poet, a partner and disease specialist at Thompsons Solicitors, said the legal outcome was welcome but emphasised that staff should not have been placed at risk in the first place.


He also raised concerns about the time taken to communicate the dangers to workers and introduce appropriate safety measures.


The case has consequently become about more than compensation. It has drawn attention to the need for healthcare employers to respond quickly when workplace hazards are identified and to ensure employees receive clear information about risks.


## Concerns About Delayed Action


An independent review conducted by the Good Governance Institute identified what it described as an unacceptable delay in the response by Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust.


According to the review, concerns about elevated gas levels had been raised in July 2021. However, the risks were not treated with the necessary seriousness until October 2022.


The report also concluded that maternity staff had been exposed to unnecessary risk or potential harm.


The Royal College of Midwives has separately highlighted concerns about the delay between identifying the problem and informing employees. Its representatives argued that workers should have been made aware of the potential danger much sooner.


Effective workplace safety depends on more than identifying a hazard. Hospitals must also assess its severity, communicate the findings to affected staff, implement protective measures and verify that those measures are working.


Where medical gases are involved, monitoring and ventilation arrangements are particularly important because employees may be exposed repeatedly during their shifts.


The incident demonstrates why clear reporting procedures and accountability are essential in healthcare settings.


## What Are the Health Risks of Nitrous Oxide Exposure?


Nitrous oxide, sometimes called laughing gas, is used in several medical settings. In maternity care, it is commonly administered as a 50:50 mixture of nitrous oxide and oxygen, often referred to as Entonox or gas and air.


It provides temporary pain relief and can help women manage discomfort and anxiety during labour.


Its established medical use should not be confused with the risks associated with repeated occupational exposure to excessive concentrations.


When gas escapes from equipment or ventilation is inadequate, nitrous oxide may accumulate in the surrounding air. Healthcare professionals who work in these environments can potentially inhale the gas over extended periods.


Prolonged or high-level exposure has been associated with neurological effects and problems involving vitamin B12 function. Vitamin B12 is important for healthy nerve function and red blood cell production, meaning disruption can have wider health consequences.


Symptoms may vary depending on the level and duration of exposure. Headaches, tiredness and difficulties with concentration can have many causes, so they should not automatically be attributed to nitrous oxide without appropriate medical assessment.


The reported experiences of staff at Basildon Hospital nevertheless underline the importance of investigating possible occupational exposure and taking appropriate action when warning signs emerge.


Importantly, the Royal College of Midwives has stressed that this case concerns workplace conditions, not the normal, properly managed use of gas and air for pain relief during labour.


## NHS Trust Responds to the Findings


Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust acknowledged that it should have acted more quickly and issued an apology to affected staff.


Louise Crosby, the trust's chief nursing and quality officer, said lessons had been learned and that oversight of medical gas monitoring across the Basildon maternity unit had been improved.


These changes are an important part of addressing the incident. However, meaningful improvements depend on ongoing monitoring, transparent communication and a willingness to investigate concerns before they develop into serious safety failures.


The Department of Health and Social Care also reiterated that patients and healthcare employees should feel safe in NHS hospitals.


A government spokesperson highlighted £271 million in funding specifically directed towards critical safety risks across NHS maternity and neonatal facilities.


The funding is intended to help address serious infrastructure problems and improve protection for mothers, babies and the professionals who care for them.


## Why Hospital Safety Must Remain a Priority


The Basildon incident has renewed calls for investment in ageing maternity facilities and more reliable ventilation systems throughout the NHS.


Hospitals rely on complex infrastructure to deliver safe care. Ventilation, medical gas pipelines, equipment maintenance and environmental monitoring may not always be visible to patients, but each plays an important role in protecting staff and the public.


When these systems fail, the consequences can extend beyond immediate operational disruption. Employees may face potential health risks, confidence in management can suffer, and resources may be diverted towards investigations, legal proceedings and remedial work.


Healthcare workers deserve an environment in which hazards are identified promptly and addressed effectively. They should also be able to raise concerns without fear that their reports will be ignored.


For maternity services in particular, protecting staff is closely connected to maintaining safe and dependable care for women and newborn babies.


The Royal College of Midwives has called for improvements not only at Basildon Hospital but also across maternity units where ventilation problems, ageing equipment or inadequate facilities may present similar challenges.


## Conclusion


The compensation settlement involving 121 NHS employees at Basildon University Hospital highlights the importance of workplace safety, timely communication and effective management of medical gases.


Although the nearly £750,000 settlement provides financial recognition for the affected workers, the wider lesson is that preventable hazards must be taken seriously from the outset.


Hospitals have a responsibility to investigate concerns, maintain safe working conditions and ensure employees understand any risks that could affect their health.


The changes introduced at Basildon Hospital, alongside wider investment in maternity infrastructure, will need sustained attention to help prevent similar incidents in the future.


Ultimately, protecting healthcare workers is an essential part of protecting patients. Safe hospitals depend on reliable equipment, suitable facilities and an organisational culture in which staff concerns lead to prompt and effective action.
